10od2uf:364: . These two sentences capture the essential difference between two kinds of automation. Traditional software automation depends on making rules explicit—you must be able to write business logic precisely as code. LLM automation, by contrast, depends on verifiability—you don’t need to write down the rules, but you must be able to judge whether the output is right or wrong. This framework explains why LLMs surge in capability in domains like math and code, where clear verification criteria exist, but fail at tasks like the “car wash problem” that humans find simple but cannot be structurally verified. It also explains the “jagged intelligence” phenomenon of LLMs. The capability distribution is not smooth; it depends on which verifiable domains RL training covers. If a domain can be engineered to generate a large number of reinforcement learning samples, the model can quickly reach expert level; if it falls outside the data distribution, the model will make mistakes even when humans regard it as common sense. The leap in chess ability from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 was not because “the model became generally smarter,” but because someone at OpenAI decided to add chess data to pretraining.

xr2kxr:293: Karpathy uses "ghost" to describe LLMs, countering a common anthropomorphic misuse: treating LLMs like animals—shouting at it makes it scared, praising it arouses intrinsic motivation. In reality, LLMs have neither emotions nor intrinsic motivation; their behavior comes entirely from statistical simulation, context, tool calls, and reward mechanisms during training. This framework has direct practical significance: don't waste emotions on the model; optimize the context and reward signals. Karpathy says he no longer memorizes API details between PyTorch, NumPy, and pandas (the model remembers them better than he does), but he must still understand the underlying concepts—what a tensor is, the relationship between views and storage, and when data is copied.
